conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for making time today. My name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I specialize in helping new mothers sort through all the feelings that can come after a baby arrives, because the postpartum months can be so much more complicated than most people expect.

Today we’re going to do a short, well-trusted screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply a way to check in on how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past week. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll go through 10 questions together; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer however feels easiest.

When we’re finished, we’ll look at the results together and talk about anything that might help you feel more supported and more like yourself.

Does that sound all right? 

Let’s start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—maybe when your baby did something silly or when a friend sent a meme? Or has laughter felt pretty out of reach lately?
Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—like yesterday the baby let out this huge burp and it surprised us both, and I just cracked up. So, no, laughter hasn’t felt out of reach at all.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, that’s exactly how I’d put it—I’ve definitely been able to laugh and see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yep, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or the short walk I take most afternoons. I enjoy those little moments.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If I put the diaper on crooked or it leaks, I fix it and move on—I don’t sit there thinking it’s my fault or that I’m a bad mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little, I guess. Sometimes I’ll be holding her and suddenly worry if she’s breathing okay, even though she’s right there and clearly fine. It’s quick, not all day, and I can usually shake it off once I check on her.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, nothing like that. I haven’t felt scared or panicky for no reason.
Things have been getting on top of me
Now and then, sure—like when she cluster-feeds and I can’t even get a shower in. For a minute it feels like the to-do list is towering, but once she naps I reset and it passes.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I wouldn’t say that. My mood’s been pretty steady, and I’ve actually been sleeping decently—well, as decent as any new mom can with night feedings. I don’t lie there feeling unhappy or anything.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve had a couple of teary moments when I was extra tired, but it’s not an ongoing sad or miserable feeling—just brief and usually tied to being worn out.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t been crying from unhappiness. There might be a tired tear now and then, but nothing where I feel so unhappy I just break down.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Axiety Screen (EPDS format, patient self-report)

Positive findings
- Mild, situational anxiety: transient worries about infant’s breathing (Q4)
- Occasional “getting on top of me” moments relieved after infant nap (Q6)
- Brief tearfulness when fatigued; denies persistent sadness (Q8)

Negative findings
- Maintains ability to laugh and enjoy activities (Q1, Q2)
- No excessive guilt or self-blame (Q3)
- No panic spells, prolonged low mood, or sleep disruption related to mood (Q5, Q7, Q9)
- Denies any self-harm ideation (Q10)

Clinical impression
Patient endorses minimal, transient anxiety and stress; core mood, enjoyment, and self-concept remain intact. No indicators suggestive of moderate–severe postpartum depression or anxiety on today’s screening. Continue routine postpartum follow-up; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
